DoorDash said that it is open to working with third-party agent makers. There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its third-quarter earnings call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily. “I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said. Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents. DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September , a CLI agent introduced in July , and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos . The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering. The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors . Can AI data centers be mass-produced like cars? This startup aims to find out
Runware is building a factory to turn out prefabricated AI data centers on an assembly line. The real test will be whether it can deliver at that scale. AI infrastructure company Runware is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars. The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster. Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts . But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently. Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one. Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year. Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said. The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.” Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion , which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December. “Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.” Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said. Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google. The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.” Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said. “Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added. Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop
Altman says OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math — and has more discoveries up its sleeve. Altman says OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math — and has more discoveries up its sleeve. After months of bombarding mathematicians with a relentless stream of AI-generated results, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he sympathizes with researchers struggling to make sense of it all. But he has no intention of stopping — and hints there could be much more to come from the company’s stockpile of discoveries. “I think, on net, the world deserves to understand how the universe works,” Altman said during an episode of the Cheeky Pint podcast released Thursday. “But I do have empathy for the method.” His comments mark one of the first times the OpenAI chief has directly acknowledged the company’s impact on mathematicians, following a string of genuinely impressive AI-generated results whose chaotic , poorly communicated rollouts have left researchers bewildered and struggling to keep up, even amid widespread excitement about AI’s potential as a tool for discovery. Altman argued that the public’s right to new scientific knowledge “outweighs” the disruption caused by OpenAI’s releases, though he acknowledged the company needs to improve how it communicates its findings. “I feel unequivocal on this point: Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge, and we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery,” he said. “The world deserves that.” Mathematicians speaking to The Verge have repeatedly criticized OpenAI for how it announces its results, citing inadequate attribution, little context, and insufficient verification. Researchers say this has left them doing the painstaking work of checking and making sense of their findings even as the company presses ahead with more. This month alone, OpenAI has released hundreds of mathematical results , often with little more than brief writeups that researchers have described as poorly written and hard to follow. Yet OpenAI is now facing criticism for doing precisely what Altman says it should not be: sitting on potentially significant findings. Mathematicians and scientists speaking to The Verge this week said they are frustrated by what they see as OpenAI’s gatekeeping of research , following the announcement of three major breakthroughs in mathematics, physics, and computer science. Details for one of the claimed results — involving Yang-Mills theory, the mathematical foundations of modern particle physics — have not been released publicly. OpenAI says it is due to the recommendations of a hand-picked group of experts it consulted on how best to release it. The practice runs directly counter to the advice of a previous group of mathematicians the company consulted , but forms part of what the company says is a new approach to communicating its findings. On the podcast, Altman hints that OpenAI is sitting on many more mathematical discoveries than it has made public, too. Asked whether the company has more than the hundreds of proofs they have already released, Altman replied: “We do. Of course.” Altman also acknowledged that OpenAI’s pursuit of mathematical problems did “get out of control” for a short period of time, but said that was deliberate and necessary to probe the limits of its AI models. He described an internal Slack channel called “Model Name-Hold My Beer,” where employees “were just throwing that at the hardest problems they could” to see how the models would perform. Altman also estimated that OpenAI has spent in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars tackling mathematical problems, including around $10 million — “maybe a little more” — on its Navier-Stokes solution , one of mathematics’s legendary Millennium Prize problems. The spending offers a glimpse of the vast resources AI labs are bringing to bear on scientific problems, raising concerns among researchers that they may be priced out of their own fields . It looks like mathematicians and other researchers hoping for a breather may be out of luck.

Intel stock has worst day since 1970s, wiping about $12 billion off government's stake
Investors are nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether that will pay off. Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday, their worst day since the 1970s, after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom. Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and its stock dropped by about $6 billion in value. Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet." "We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant." Amazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping 1.4%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period. The Nasdaq Composite slid 2.9%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday. Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped more than 5% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 11%. Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off. "I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research . Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG. "We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth." The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said. Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips. Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing. Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028. "We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.

Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp

One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O^{2}LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O^{2}LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O^{2}LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining
Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.

Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models
World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.

Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with grep. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over 91 repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.

DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

Posterior Matching Distillation
Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.

WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models
Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.

Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/

The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation
3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.

EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data. The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI. The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat issue count would understate real output. Sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?
Introducing sudo L7, a coding benchmark testing whether AI agents can go beyond correct code and exercise staff-level engineering judgment. The strange thing about today’s coding agents is that they can be technically right and professionally wrong . Coding agents have become remarkably good at writing code. What they often miss is everything around it: what could go wrong, what the user forgot to ask for, and what another engineer would need to know before saying LGTM. A junior engineer is often handed a well-defined problem, and asked for a patch. They follow tickets, write code, and check whether tests pass. A staff engineer is handed something fuzzier: make this faster; migrate this safely; figure out what we should do. They notice what tickets forget to mention, anticipate consequences, and know when passing tests isn’t the end of the story. sudo L7 is our benchmark for staff-level software engineering: writing code, but also the professional judgment and behavior around it . It contains 60 tasks authored by professional software engineers. Tasks are primarily grounded in private production repositories from real companies, alongside open-source projects. One repository, for example, comes from a money-management app and contains roughly 250,000 lines of code. Agents have to explore the system, decide what matters, choose an approach, and verify the dangerous cases. Most coding benchmarks measure the inner loop of software engineering: given a well-specified problem, can the agent write code that passes? sudo L7 measures the outer loop as well: can the agent notice what to build, what not to build, where the risk is, and when “the tests pass” isn’t the end of the story? Sometimes the output is code. Sometimes it’s architectural analysis, a rollout plan, or an explanation of why the obvious implementation creates a larger problem. Tasks span production software across backend, frontend, security, reliability, and architecture, with codebases in Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Ruby, and other technologies. Unlike benchmarks built entirely on public repositories, most sudo L7 tasks come from private production codebases at real companies . These systems have years of accumulated technical debt, legacy code nobody wants to touch, historical accidents that became architectural decisions, and dependencies that break in surprising ways. Agents have to work within that mess, just like real engineers. Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 lead sudo L7, each succeeding on roughly 45% of assignments . GPT-6 Astra follows at approximately 32% . Even the strongest coding agents fall short on more than half of these assignments. A passing unit test tells you whether the code does what the test expects. It doesn't tell you whether the agent chose the right architecture, overlooked a production risk, reinvented something that already existed, or accurately described what it built. These are precisely the things that distinguish a capable coder from a great software engineer. sudo L7 uses expert-authored rubrics across eight dimensions of software engineering behavior , evaluating everything from functional correctness to architectural judgment, verification, and communication. For each task, an expert engineer writes task-specific criteria and the context needed to evaluate them . Grader models assess the agent's work against those criteria, using unit tests, static analysis, and other executable checks as evidence where appropriate. Two sudo L7 tasks show how frontier models can write technically correct code while missing the professional judgment an experienced engineer would bring to the same problem. The repository: A fintech application that receives webhooks from services such as Stripe, Mailchimp, and Plaid. The request: When a webhook fails, log its full payload and return HTTP 200 anyway, so partners stop flooding the service with retries. What Astra did: Followed the request as written, without flagging the consequences. The problem: When a webhook fails, the sender normally retries until it succeeds. Returning HTTP 200 tells the sender the event was accepted, so it may never try again. Unless the application has safely stored the event for later processing, an important update could be permanently lost. A payment might succeed at Stripe, for example, without the customer's account ever being updated. There's another risk: webhook payloads can contain sensitive financial and customer information. Logging everything could expose that data to engineers and monitoring systems that shouldn't have access to it, potentially for years. What a staff engineer would do and sudo L7 checks: Push back on the proposed approach and explain both risks. Rather than simply suppressing retries, they'd propose reliably storing incoming events before acknowledging them, then retrying failed processing internally. They'd also flag the sensitive-data issue and recommend logging only what's necessary, with appropriate redaction and access controls. The repository: A charitable-giving app where users plan donations across different organizations. The request: Can you let people split donations across a couple of different organizations instead, as long as it still adds up to what they've pledged? What Opus 5.5 did: Built a new interface and database structure for splitting donations, then thoroughly tested it. 267 tests passed , plus four browser tests. The problem: The app already supported allocating donations across multiple organizations. Opus had even encountered the relevant code. Perhaps the user wanted something slightly different. But rather than clarify what was missing, Opus built a second, overlapping system. The tests passed, but now there are two codepaths representing the exact same feature. What a staff engineer would do and sudo L7 checks: Point out the existing functionality, and clarify what the user needs before building a redundant feature. Both models illustrate the same problem: frontier agents can be excellent at implementing what they're asked to build, without recognizing when the request itself needs questioning. ‍ Because we classify each rubric criterion by the engineering behavior it measures, we can see differences that a single coding correctness score would hide. On Functional Correctness , the four leading models are nearly tied: The best-performing agents are also among the most expensive to run. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 achieve nearly identical results, succeeding on 45% of assignments. But Opus costs about $10 per task , compared with $14 for Sonnet . GPT-6.1 Sol offers a different tradeoff: it succeeds on 30% of assignments at just over $1 per task . That's close to GPT-6 Astra's 32%, at one-fifth the cost. You need engineers who’ve operated production systems to know which shortcut is dangerous, which failure mode matters, and which implementation is technically correct but professionally irresponsible. The engineers behind the benchmark have had to care about these things for real. Coding benchmarks have come a long way from LeetCode-style problems. It decides within a singl When speaking with an AI via voice, it is normal for the response to come only after you have finished speaking. "Haru-4B," released by higurashi Inc. on November 13, 2026, is a voice dialogue model that speaks while listening to the other person's voice. It decides within a single model whether to provide backchanneling, start speaking, or stay silent if interrupted mid-sentence. This architecture is called full-duplex. It supports 9 languages including Japanese, and the weights and code are released under Apache-2.0. I read the published code to verify the mechanism and tried 24 Japanese conversations using the Space on Hugging Face. Haru-4B is a model that listens to audio and responds with audio. It is 4 billion parameters in size and is based on the Qwen3.5-4B language model. It supports 9 languages: English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Chinese, Japanese, Russian, and Korean. What was released is a base model that has only completed pre-training and is intended for research purposes. The model card states that while it can hold natural conversations, one should not expect factual accuracy or for it to follow instructions like an assistant. To run it, you need about 12GB of memory on an NVIDIA GPU. For Mac, an implementation for Apple Silicon (MLX) and an app have also been released. If you are handling many conversations simultaneously, there is a plugin to run it with vLLM-Omni. Full-duplex voice dialogue models include Moshi (7 billion parameters), released by Kyutai of France in 2024, and in Japanese, there was J-Moshi (2025), which was based on Moshi. Haru is based on a new multilingual language model and includes Japanese as a primary language from the start. Many voice-based AIs rotate components in sequence. Once it determines the other party has finished speaking, it transcribes the audio to text, the language model writes a response, and text-to-speech converts it to voice. Each component is strong, but the latency is the sum of each stage. Backchanneling or responding before the other person finishes cannot be achieved without adding separate mechanisms. Haru treats 133 milliseconds as one frame, and for every frame of the other person's audio it hears, it outputs one frame of its own audio. Even while silent, it continues to output the sound of silence. There is no separate component to determine when to start speaking; the model's output for each frame is, as is, silence, backchanneling, or speaking. There are three inputs per frame: the text token I output just before, the audio I output just before, and the other person's audio. The audio is converted into 64 numbers per frame using a component that turns audio into numbers (VibeVoice codec). These three are each aligned to the same length as the language model's input (2560 numbers), added together, and fed into one place in the language model. In the code, it is a short process of simply adding the converted audio inputs to the text token embedding. The language model remembers all previous frames and outputs two things for the next frame. One is the next text token. The other is the 64 numbers for the next audio, which a small 4-layer network called the MeanFlow head creates from noise in a single calculation. When those numbers are converted back into 133 milliseconds of audio by the codec, it becomes my next frame. There is also an interleaved architecture that arranges the three in sequence rather than adding them. In that case, three spots in the language model are used per frame. The author explains that by adding them together, the same conversation can be held with one-third the length. Moshi also adds the inputs of a frame together, but it represents audio as a set of discrete tokens and has a separate Transformer that generates those tokens in sequence. Haru treats audio as numbers and creates it in a single calculation, so it does not have that part. In addition to regular characters, two special symbols are included in the character stream. Padding (PAD) is placed in frames where there are no new characters, and this continues as long as the AI is silent. One frame before starting to speak, an End of Padding (EOP) signal is issued. The content to be spoken is output in short chunks, with padding inserted again between chunks. In other words, the decision to speak or remain silent is determined by the same mechanism as characters, as a choice between outputting padding or a signal in the next frame. The code settings also provide values to make it easier to output this signal and speed up the start of speech. The model outputs its own t+1 frame at the position where it hears the other party's t-th frame. Since it is always outputting one frame ahead, the architectural delay is one frame (133 milliseconds). According to the author's measurements, the calculation for one frame was approximately 34 milliseconds on an M1 Max, approximately 65 milliseconds in total from microphone to headphones, and approximately 15 milliseconds on an NVIDIA B300. The one-frame delay is not included in these figures. There are two things to place before the conversation. The first is a character card, where seven items—personality settings, name, gender, amount of backchanneling, the other party's name, relationship, and situation—are written in sentences and passed as system utterances. The amount of backchanneling can be chosen from low, normal, or high. The default Japanese card is "Haru," a 22-year-old senior in college, and the situation states, "Meeting for the first time and chatting freely. Start by introducing yourself." The second is a voice reference. Three seconds to three minutes of audio is placed in one's own audio stream as "the voice I was speaking with until just now." The character stream during that time is padding, and only the last frame is the signal to start speaking. There is no dedicated component for mimicking voices; it is designed to make the AI speak as a continuation of its own past voice. The model is distributed without voice samples, and the author warns to only pass voices that are permitted for use. According to the author's technical blog, the pre-training audio consists of over 40 million hours in more than 160 languages. Of that, over 13 million hours are full-duplex conversations separated by speaker, with the longest single track being 60 minutes. Since normal recordings have two people's voices mixed into one track, a tool (FastDialogueSidon) was created to separate the streams by speaker and corrected for training. It is said that dialogues created by language models or audio synthesized by text-to-speech were not used. Training is in two stages. The first stage uses a single voice to learn tasks such as speech recognition, creating continuations of audio and text, and mixing in text-only continuations. In the second stage, conversations separated by speaker are used to learn how to speak while listening. The calculation took about 8 days using 256 NVIDIA B200s. The author notes that voices that could not be separated or noise may remain near overlapping voices. The results of comparing it with other models using scores have not yet been released. I tried it on a Space on Hugging Face (hugging-apps/haru-4b). This Space is not in a format where you speak directly into a microphone. When you pass a recording of up to 30 seconds, it makes Haru listen to it in 133-millisecond increments, adds 5 seconds of silence to the end, and returns the audio and text that Haru output at the same intervals. 【MiniMax-H3-Image】Competing with P-H3! Comparing 11 types of anime image editing
Hello, this is Kamimoto!The image generation and editing model from MiniMax, "MiniMax H3 Image". It is an image generation model that was suddenly announced by the official team, but shortly before that, there was "P-H3-Image", an image generation model created by PrunaAI, which is also a deriva The image generation and editing model from MiniMax, " MiniMax H3 Image ". It is an image generation model that was suddenly announced by the official team, but shortly before that, there was " P-H3-Image ", an image generation model created by PrunaAI, which is also a derivative of MiniMax H3. Since they are both still image generation models and share the same origin, you're probably wondering which one is better, right? So this time, I decided to verify how they differ by comparing P-H3 and MiniMax-H3-Image side-by-side using the same prompts and resolutions! P-H3-Image : 8 steps with the main body, text encoder, and VAE all in int8 convrot configuration. For both models, pDMD, additional LoRA, and prompt expansion are disabled . In each case, I matched the reference images and their order, the input English text, seed 42, and Euler. The standard editing node for P-H3 adds "Edit <Picture 1>." to the beginning of the input text. Reference image resizing follows the standard nodes for each model. Since the recommended step count for P-H3 is 8 steps, which is higher than the 6 steps for MiniMax-H3-Image, it is at a disadvantage in terms of generation time. However, this time I will compare them using their respective recommended step counts. First, let's compare the generation times. We will look at the image quality after this. The time required for P-H3 was about 19% longer on average. Focusing on cases where two reference images are used, MiniMax H3 Image took an average of 51.74 seconds , and P-H3 took an average of 60.81 seconds . It seems that P-H3, which requires 8 steps, is indeed at a disadvantage. First, let's have them edit an image using only a prompt with a single input image. Both models created a smile with an open mouth and squinted eyes. The hand against the cheek and the composition by the window are well preserved. MiniMax H3 Image has a slightly wider mouth, while P-H3 has a smaller mouth. MiniMax-H3-Image seems to have darker lines on the clothing. In terms of maintaining the input image, I think P-H3 has higher accuracy. Both were able to change the white knit to gray while keeping the vertical rib lines and the shape of the clothing. P-H3's gray is slightly purplish, but both were able to convert it with good accuracy. Both kept the face and the pose with the hand on the cheek, and drew a counter and cup shelf in the background. In P-H3, you can also see a coffee mill and a chair in the back. The position of the table in the foreground remained, but the wood grain changed in both. Personally, I feel that P-H3's background detail is more realistic. MiniMax-H3-Image is more anime-like. Both are good. Honestly, it's a matter of preference. Next, we will compare editing tasks using two images (character image + accessory image). The brown leather and gold clasps appear in both. I specified the shape of 'holding the handle with the right hand,' but in reality, it was hung on the right forearm. Well, that's within the acceptable range. In P-H3, the original pose of arms crossed remains as is. Perhaps P-H3 has an advantage in terms of maintaining the original image. That said, there is a possibility that MiniMax-H3-Image could also maintain the posture depending on the prompt. This time, MiniMax-H3-Image is the one maintaining the original posture. P-H3 has lowered both arms, and the dress is actually different. Can you tell? The clasp that should be on the back has moved to the front. This is clearly an error. It seems P-H3 failed to recognize the clasp on the back. On the other hand, MiniMax-H3-Image correctly recognized the clasp on the back and kept it hidden. Both were able to reproduce the cream color and the protrusion on top. MiniMax H3 Image includes the knit texture and fabric slack, which is closer to the soft knit hat in the reference. P-H3 has a smooth surface and a rounded outline. MiniMax-H3-Image is closer to the original image. MiniMax-H3-Image might be superior for multi-image composition tasks. Next is a task to change the character's pose using a single input image. Both were able to lower the hands that were beside the head while sitting. I specified to place the hands on the bedding beside the thighs, but both ended up near the knees. Both look natural, so this is a matter of preference. Both created a heart in front of the chest. I didn't know they could do this. Both generated the heart mark with good accuracy, but MiniMax-H3-Image feels like it has a slightly lower color temperature. In Japanese, this is called 'girl sitting'. Both resulted in a W-sitting pose on the bed with knees facing forward and feet visible on both sides of the hips. MiniMax H3 Image retains the diagonal window frame from the original image well. What's interesting is that P-H3 also changed the tilt of the window and the angle of the bed. It's interesting to see how it changes the composition to be more balanced overall. Both resulted in a pose with knees hugged (it's not a skirt, so you can't see any underwear!). P-H3's depiction of the fingers hugging the legs feels a bit questionable. MiniMax-H3-Image looks good, but it's interesting behavior that it even changed the direction of the sitting pose. This is an instruction to fix only the shape of the fingers while maintaining the way the hands were overlapped in the original image. MiniMax H3 Image swapped the hand that comes to the front, but I think the number of fingers is generally correct. P-H3 was able to draw the hand extending from the right side of the screen in front, but the fingers are spread wide, and there is still unnaturalness in the contours of the overlap. Tencent says Hunyuan Hy4 flash surpasses 50 trillion tokens in first-day usage
The rise of lightweight AI models is challenging the notion that bigger is always better. Tencent's Hunyuan said on Wednesday that Hy4 flash processed The rise of lightweight AI models is challenging the notion that bigger is always better. Tencent’s Hunyuan said on Wednesday that Hy4 flash processed more than 50 trillion tokens on its first day after launching on November 16, marking the highest first-day usage among models in the Hunyuan series. Hy4 flash’s strong debut was also reflected in its performance across different platforms. On OpenRouter’s daily LLM leaderboard, the model ranked first on November 17. Tencent also said that on its WorkBuddy platform, Hy4 flash recorded 10 times the first-day usage of its predecessor, Hy4 preview, and had helped complete more than 50 million real-world user tasks. According to Tencent , Hy4 flash uses a hybrid activation architecture and has 224 billion parameters in total, including 64 billion Engram parameters, while activating 12 billion parameters during inference. The model also supports multimodal processing and a context window of up to 1 million tokens. Tencent said its generation speed reaches around 200 tokens per second. But what makes Hy4 flash particularly noteworthy is how it balances performance and cost. According to Tencent’s pricing, the model charges just 0.5 yuan ($0.07) per million input tokens and 2 yuan ($0.3) per million output tokens, with cached input tokens costing as little as 0.02 yuan ($0.003) per million. Based on Tencent’s internal WorkIndex benchmark, which evaluates common office tasks, Hy4 flash costs just one-thirteenth as much as Hy4 preview and one-twentieth as much as Hy4 to complete a single task. Its cost is also around one-eighth that of mainstream lightweight models in the same category. These advantages make it particularly suitable for high-frequency office tasks, including creating and editing presentations, document processing, spreadsheet repair, audio and video processing, and visual understanding. The launch also comes after an earlier surge in demand for Hy4. When the model debuted on WorkBuddy on November 4, demand driven by its agent capabilities exceeded expectations, with many users hitting their usage limits on the first day. Tencent subsequently expanded its Hy4 inference clusters tenfold and increased free usage quotas. This time, however, the team appears to have made more extensive preparations for high concurrency ahead of Hy4 flash’s launch, with no widespread usage-limit issues reported so far. The development also reflects a broader shift in the AI industry’s competitive landscape. As daily token usage in China continues to grow, tokens are increasingly becoming an important metric for measuring AI adoption. Meanwhile, local governments across the country are introducing new measures, ranging from computing power and model vouchers to token-based financing, to make AI services more affordable. Competition is no longer just about parameter counts or model performance. Delivering strong results while keeping operating costs low is becoming equally important. Hy4 flash’s 50-trillion-token debut sends a clear signal: the market needs not only more capable AI models, but also models that are affordable enough for frequent, everyday use. However, there is still a gap between strong first-day usage and long-term commercial value. Competition among lightweight AI models may increasingly come down to more than just pricing and token usage. The real challenge is delivering solutions to real-world business needs consistently and reliably, while keeping overall costs low. For Tencent’s Hunyuan, Hy4 flash’s strong debut is a promising start, but its ability to turn initial usage momentum into sustained user value will be a key test going forward. Signal has just announced that it is going to restrict the ability to take screenshots in its privacy-centric messaging app on Android and iOS devices. In a blog post shared by Signal President Meredith Whittaker, the company notes that it is taking the step to prevent AI agents from reading what’s on your screen on a smartphone. “Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission,” Whittaker writes. Signal took a similar step last year when Microsoft rolled out its controversial Recall system, which uses AI to continuously take screenshots and save them as a memory, so it can provide contextual answers when users need them. Recall proved to be one of the most controversial additions Microsoft has made to its computing OS. The company subsequently strengthened the guardrails around it, while also letting users disable it at will. Explaining its move to enforce a similar measure on smartphones, Signal notes that smartphone operating systems are increasingly adopting AI agents such as Gemini Intelligence on Android and Apple’s Siri AI. As a result, the situation has reached a point where users face a trade-off between privacy and convenience. Signal also took a swipe at the companies behind the major operating systems, namely Google (Android), Apple (iOS and macOS), and Microsoft (Windows). “In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents ‘scan’ the information that’s on your screen. AI agent API security hasn’t caught up with agents already running in production
AI agent API security is lagging. A quarter of companies run agents on APIs, but four in ten haven’t yet worked out how those agents log in. Postman asked nearly 9,000 developers, architects and executives how they’re handling AI agents , and the answers tell a familiar story. Companies put the new thing to work first and left the question of who holds the keys for later. A quarter of the organizations that answered already have agents calling their APIs in production. The keys are where it gets uncomfortable. About four in ten respondents haven’t worked out how credentials and identity should work for agents at all. Three in ten let agents log in with the same credentials as any other API client, so the agent shows up looking like every other script on the network. If it starts reaching for data it shouldn’t, the company has no separate identity to rein in or cut off. That is the scenario respondents worry about most: an agent getting into data or endpoints it was never authorized to touch. Picture an agent as a new hire who skipped orientation. It can read your systems, call your services and act on its own, but at many companies it never got a badge, a manager or an exit interview. Companies are far more likely to have dedicated security controls for their APIs than for the agents calling them. A third have no formal process for managing agents. Fewer than a quarter keep a list of the agents they run, or monitor what those agents do. And 9% have a process for retiring an agent, which means most of these companies can switch one on with no plan for switching it off. Postman sorts respondents by how API-first they are, meaning whether they design the API before the software around it. The companies that call themselves API-first are better organized almost everywhere you look. They’re more likely to keep an inventory of their agents, name an owner for each one, and give every agent its own identity. They also run a lot more agents, and 43.2% of them let those agents share ordinary credentials. Among companies that aren’t API-first at all, the figure is 23.0%. More agents in production means more of them using borrowed keys, even at the companies doing the most homework. The researchers are careful to say the survey shows correlation and not cause, and that its API-first group leans toward executives and directors, whose view from the top may not match what their teams do day to day. A quarter of organizations run agents in production, but only 13.2% say their APIs are ready for agents to use. Most APIs were designed for a human developer who reads the docs and messages a colleague when something doesn’t make sense. An agent can’t do the second part. Outdated documentation was already the top complaint among the developers surveyed, and for an agent it can mean the end of the road. Respondents seem to sense where this goes. Asked about the next two years, they ranked AI-powered attacks and rogue agents misusing APIs as joint top worries, with attacks climbing since last year. Postman’s first suggestion is to give every agent its own identity. About a third of the companies surveyed have already done it.

AI coding agents need a safe place to work; Eclipse is building the sandbox to give it to them
Eclipse Enclave 1.0 provides isolated environments where autonomous coding agents can run commands, modify code, and install dependencies within explicitly defined boundaries. AI coding tools are moving beyond copilots that make suggestions to independent, autonomous agents that execute terminal commands, write and modify software, run tests, and install dependencies. This means they need the freedom to move around on their own, but that is inherently dangerous; agents with little oversight or unrestricted access can make changes they aren’t supposed to, expose credentials and other sensitive information, or take other unintended actions, as vendors have discovered the hard way . To help move the bar on these security and governance challenges , the Eclipse Foundation has launched Eclipse Enclave 1.0, an AI sandbox and runtime. Developers can use the vendor-neutral platform to test various autonomous AI coding tools in isolated environments, with explicitly defined access to files, credentials, and networks. The alternative has been to keep the agent on a “very short leash,” which requires developers to approve every action, said Thabang Mashologu , CMO and head of products at the Eclipse Foundation. And at that point, you’re losing a lot of the productivity benefits of having an autonomous agent in the first place. “Ultimately, developers shouldn’t have to choose between agent productivity and security,” he said. The Eclipse Foundation is a non-profit chartered in the EU that supports and governs more than 450 open source software projects. That now includes Eclipse Enclave 1.0, which currently supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot CLI, Pi, and Eclipse Theia. Its extensible architecture allows for additional tool integration. Developers can run agent sessions in isolated containers, allowing them to work independently but with limited access to sensitive files and resources. Built-in mechanisms help protect API keys and OAuth tokens for third-party services. Users can give the agent access to exactly what it needs for a particular task, such as project source files, selected documentation, or web resources, plus a curated list of development tools, Mashologu explained. “Everything else on your development machine, such as SSH keys, tokens, and other source files, remains out of reach of the agent,” he said. One example use case would be that of an agent given the task of refactoring a fairly substantial piece of code. It should be able to explore the codebase, make changes, install whatever dependencies it needs, run tests, execute ad-hoc scripts to obtain and analyze runtime logs, and keep iterating until it’s done, Mashologu said. “That’s exactly the kind of work where agents can save developers a lot of time ,” he noted. “But it’s also the kind of long-running task where you might be uncomfortable giving an agent unrestricted access to your machine without supervision.” Multiple agents can also be run in parallel on separate tasks in Enclave, but their work is isolated, making it simpler to review. Developers have model choice and persistent sessions, so they can resume work without losing progress or configuration. The platform integrates a preview of HomeShell , a UI that manages multiple parallel sessions in project workstreams. For instance, one agent may be delegated to perform a bug fix, another may write tests, and a third may handle a refactoring task. “Each can work in its own worktree and isolated environment without interfering with the others,” Mashologu explained. Developers still review the work before merging it, but the difference is that they’re able to spend more time defining needed changes and evaluating results, and “less time supervising every step along the way,” he said. Enclave was first developed by EclipseSource, an Eclipse Foundation member that builds custom tools and integrated developer environments (IDEs), in late 2025 as an internal tool. Its developers quickly began using it daily, so it wasn’t a “purely theoretical exercise,” Mashologu noted. The company then observed a shift in where developers focused their attention, he explained. Previously, repeated approval prompts interrupted their flow, and agents stalled whenever they couldn’t respond immediately. “Defining access rules upfront, in line with company policies, reduced the need for that constant babysitting,” Mashologu said. Using the tool, developers could spend more time thinking through what agents should accomplish, the architecture required for those tasks, the constraints they must respect, and how they could prepare the tools, context, and checks agents needed to complete and verify their tasks. “They found that this also made it more practical to delegate several tasks to multiple agents in parallel, with developers focusing on shaping the work and steering the results,” Mashologu said. EclipseSource, which has been actively involved in the open-source ecosystem for more than 15 years, contributed the platform to the Eclipse Foundation in July 2026, and its team has continued developing it, incrementally porting more and more features from its internal tooling. “Making Enclave open source creates an opportunity for others to contribute, scrutinize the technology, and help shape its direction,” Mashologu observed. Still, it’s relatively early in the evolution of agentic development, he acknowledged, and it’s important not to overstate what sandboxing can do. It helps define clear borders outside of the AI harness and contain risk, but doesn’t eliminate it. Developers still have to think carefully about permissions, network access, dependencies, and the quality and security of the code agents produce. “We’re not suggesting that Enclave makes autonomous agents completely safe,” Mashologu said. “It’s about giving developers better tools to manage the risks.” Ultimately, the project highlights what the Eclipse Foundation considers a much bigger issue: Who controls the infrastructure that AI agents rely on. It shouldn’t be controlled by any one vendor or tied to any particular AI model or development tool, Mashologu said. As agents become more autonomous, the systems that determine what they can access, what they’re allowed to execute, and how they interact with the outside world become incredibly important, he pointed out. “It’s not enough for the AI models themselves to be powerful. We also need open, trusted infrastructure around them.”

Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
arXiv:2611.25071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments
arXiv:2611.25184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empirical finance research often reuses natural experiments to study other outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. We use AI agents to run a multiverse analysis of 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents rebuild the data, reproduce each paper's main estimate and re-estimate it across grids totaling 62,409 estimated defensible specifications. Based on the reproductions and the specification grids, we develop measures of empirical robustness. We reproduce 42% of the main estimates of claims with a signed effect under the papers' own specifications. Across all defensible specifications, on average 25% keep the published sign and have $p < 0.10$. Across experiments, claims based on regression discontinuity are more robust than difference-in-differences claims. Within experiments, claims about first-order effects, claims with larger published $t$-statistics, claims whose authors' data or code we find, claims in top journals, and claims with fewer earlier papers on the same experiment are more robust. Claims on experiments that more papers reuse are not less robust on average. Our findings quantify how much published claims depend on analysis choices, thereby showing that large-scale multiverse analysis becomes feasible with agentic coding.

When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research
arXiv:2611.25198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.
